title: The Night Out
dek: Social venues sell the experience even as drinking itself declines.
lede: The bar and nightclub business is bigger than ever—$38.6 billion in 2026—but it's not about the drink anymore. Gen Z is ordering less alcohol, older drinkers are aging out, and younger people are cutting back even as they still go out. The money is moving to the venue itself: the design, the staff, the vibe, the event. Bars that just serve drinks are running out of customers. Bars that offer an experience are where the growth is.
what_changed:
The bars and nightclubs industry is splitting into two completely different businesses. On one side, you have upscale experiential venues—craft cocktail lounges, themed bars, wine bars with staff guidance and events—that are growing and pushing margins back up. On the other side, the traditional neighborhood bar selling cheap drinks is shrinking. The industry was $26.7 billion in 2022 and grew to $38.6 billion by 2026, but that growth is entirely concentrated in the premium experience tier. Themed bar venues surged 32.9% in 2025 alone. Experiential dining venues—restaurants offering pop-ups, chef experiences, immersive design—jumped 46% year-over-year, with restaurants adding 34% more experiences. Wine bars grew 6.8% annually when led by private-equity operators investing in the experience side, but traditional independent wine bars face collapsing margins.

The real shift is in who's drinking. U.S. adult drinking rates hit 54% in August 2025, the lowest in 90 years. Gen Z drinks 30% less than Millennials did at the same age. Monthly wine occasions among Gen Z have collapsed 34% since 2019. At the same time, GLP-1 medications (now used by 10–15% of U.S. adults) reduce on-premise alcohol spending by 30% and home spending by 22%. Even when younger drinkers do go out, they're ordering fewer drinks—3.9 per occasion in 2025 versus 4.4 in 2024—but they spend more per drink on premium options. This is called "selective premiumization": fewer drinks, better quality, higher price. The younger audience still shows up; they're just not there to drink. They're there for the night out.

Costs are squeezing the middle. Labor is brutal—a typical nightclub spends $70,416 per month on staff wages, and bartender turnover runs 50–70% annually, driving constant rehiring costs. Imported spirits tariffs pushed premium bottle prices up 15–20% by mid-2026. Domestic spirits face their own inflation from grain costs and aged-barrel constraints. Venues have to pass some of this to customers, but pricing power only works at the top. The low-end venue—the dive bar, the cheap nightclub—can't raise prices without losing what's left of its younger customer base. These venues are stuck between rising costs and a customer base that's drinking less and has less disposable income.

Private equity is consolidating chains. Sun Holdings bought Bar Louie in 2025, signaling that PE sees scale and the ability to standardize the "experience" as the playbook. The fragmented industry—70,000 venues with no chain exceeding 5% market share—is vulnerable to roll-up. Operators who can build a consistent themed environment, hire and retain trained staff, manage premium pricing, and create social media-worthy moments are winning. Operators who rely on volume and cheap drinks are losing.

win: Private-equity-led upscale venues, craft cocktail bars, and experiential nightclubs—places where the venue itself is the draw. Operators who invest in immersive design, trained staff, themed events, and social media moments are seeing 6.8% growth (in wine bars) and 32.9% surge in themed venues. Older, affluent drinkers (55+) who can afford premium prices and don't face medical restrictions are still spending. Non-alcoholic premium experiences—mocktails, soft clubbing in daytime spaces—grew 36% and tap into the younger customer without the health and cost friction.
lose: Traditional independent bars and casual chains selling cheap drinks. Margins fell from 6.8% to 5.4% industry-wide, but are worse for venues betting on volume. Younger, price-sensitive drinkers—already cutting back due to health and wallet tightness—can't afford 15–20% price hikes from tariffs on premium spirits. Gen Z wine occasions collapsed 34% since 2019. Bartenders and entry-level staff face wage inflation ($70k monthly lab for a typical venue) and constant turnover, making the low-margin neighborhood bar uneconomical. Venues relying on imported premium spirits face tariff and supply-chain volatility.
worry: The structural demand wall is real and accelerating. U.S. adult drinking rates hit a 90-year low in August 2025. Gen Z drinks 30% less than the generation before at the same age, and GLP-1 adoption (now 10–15% of adults) is reducing on-premise spending by 30%. Even when younger people go out, they're not ordering drinks—they're ordering the experience. If the experience becomes too expensive, or if younger drinkers continue to age out of drinking habits, the entire on-premise alcohol industry faces a demand floor that's hard to engineer around. The 2025 Dietary Guidelines removed explicit daily drink limits, but the U.S. Surgeon General simultaneously issued an advisory linking alcohol to nearly 100,000 annual cancer cases. This mixed messaging will keep younger people cautious. The consolidation into upscale venues could leave entire regions underserved—if the only profitable bar is the $20-cocktail place, what happens to social venues for ordinary people?
one_sentence: People are going out, but they're not going out to drink—they're going out for the experience, which means venues that sell atmosphere and events are thriving while traditional bars betting on volume are squeezed.

title: Play & Compete
dek: Bowling centers and go-kart tracks pivot from equipment rentals to multi-hour paid social experiences, remaking the afternoon into an event.
lede: Bowling used to be a weekend league thing—reserved lanes, same people, same shoes. Go-kart racing was a field trip or birthday party. Now both industries are in the middle of a structural flip: they're no longer selling you the activity alone, they're selling you the night out. The money is moving from hourly lane rental to food, drinks, laser tag, arcade games, and VR scoring overlays. Bowling centers are consolidating into premium social venues; go-kart tracks are adding electric racing, VR arenas, and targeting families and women instead of just teenage boys.
what_changed:
The bowling industry itself is shrinking—the number of bowling centers dropped from 3,165 to 2,484 between 2021 and 2026, a 2.1% annual decline. But the survivors are getting bigger and wealthier. Bowlero Corporation rebranded itself Lucky Strike Entertainment in December 2024, trading publicly on the NYSE under ticker LUCK. That move says it all: bowling is no longer the product, social experience is. In fiscal 2024, Bowlero spent $145.9 million acquiring eight locations, including 14 Lucky Strike centers and a water park. The company is consolidating lanes under a single upscale brand while aggressively diversifying revenue. At a surviving bowling center today, bowling revenue now comprises only 45–60% of total income—the rest comes from food, beverages, laser tag, arcade games, and event hosting. Centers with advanced technology like AR/VR lane scoring report 20% higher customer retention. About 22% of new bowling openings now feature interactive scoring and augmented reality. The margin profile is shifting too: traditional single-location bowling alleys still operate on thin 10–15% net margins, but rebranded entertainment centers built around bowling are capturing 20–35% EBITDA, with the top venues approaching 30% net margins.

The go-kart industry is younger and smaller but following a similar playbook. The market was $185 million in 2025, growing at 12.3% CAGR from 2020–2025—nearly double the bowling growth rate. But growth is flattening: 2026 is projected to add only 1.6%. Indoor facilities now dominate 67% of the market share, up from near parity a few years ago, because they operate year-round and can charge reliably. K1 Speed, the largest operator, acquired Autobahn Indoor Speedway (11 locations) in January 2024 and Capital Karts in May 2024, signaling consolidation similar to Bowlero's strategy. The industry is racing to electrify—electric go-karts reached 53.4% of equipment sales in 2024, cutting operating costs and removing emissions headaches in indoor urban locations. Pole Position Raceway and others are investing $10 million-plus in electric infrastructure. But the real growth vector is not the karts themselves; it's the experience wrapper. Venues are bolting on Omni Arena by Virtuix (full-body VR racing), esports tournaments, and event spaces to capture the full night-out economics. Go-kart racing demographics are also shifting: the industry has historically skewed 81% young male, but venues are explicitly targeting older participants and female guests as a strategic priority.

What this force made scarce: traditional bowling-centric communities and single-venue local operators. Traditional bowling still has league players, but the economic model no longer supports standalone alleys. What it made cheap: the marginal experience add-on. Once you've driven someone to the venue, feeding her and giving her a VR upsell costs the venue almost nothing incremental—margins are fat. What it made risky: the small operator model and suburban single-location businesses that can't afford $10 million electric infrastructure or AR/VR upgrades. What it made newly valuable: licensed experience brands (Lucky Strike), urban and family-friendly environments, food and beverage integration, technology stacks that work on older equipment, and female and older-adult participation metrics.

win: Consolidated operators with scale to invest in technology and real estate see fat margins. Bowlero/Lucky Strike's shift to upscale, multi-use venues is capturing 20–35% EBITDA margins by upselling food, drinks, and entertainment to the captive crowd. K1 Speed and similar go-kart networks can absorb the $10 million-plus capital investment in electric infrastructure and still grow. Urban venues in major metros benefit from density and higher spend-per-visit. Younger demographics (18–34) seeking memorable social experiences—not ownership—spend freely on venue visits when technology and environment match their taste.
lose: Small single-location bowling alleys and independent go-kart rental shops cannot afford technology upgrades, brand investment, or food and beverage integration. Traditional league players see their bowling identity absorbed into generic entertainment venues. Suburbs with one aging bowling center or kart track will watch it close or get acquired and rebranded. Smaller go-kart operators outside consolidation networks face rising electric infrastructure costs without scale to recoup them. The 81% male skew in go-kart racing reflects an inability of independent operators to invest in female-focused marketing or family programming.
worry: Consumer leisure spending is beginning to show real strain. Go-kart revenue growth dropped from 12.3% CAGR (2020–2025) to just 1.6% projected in 2026 as post-pandemic savings depletes and credit card debt rises, particularly for younger demographics. If consumer spending on experiences contracts, the entire model—high-margin food and entertainment upsells—depends on keeping people inside the venue for longer and making them spend repeatedly. Economic downturn could flip the rebranding strategy from strength to vulnerability: a $20 million investment in a premium experience brand becomes a liability if customers cut discretionary spending.
one_sentence: Bowling centers and go-kart tracks are consolidating into branded entertainment experiences with food, drinks, and VR stacked on top of the core game, capturing 20–35% margins and abandoning the small-operator model.

title: Theme Parks & Thrills
dek: Big-ticket days out keep pricing power as families trade goods for memories.
lede: Amusement parks in America are booming by the numbers—$33.4 billion in 2026, up nearly 10% a year—but something underneath feels like a squeeze. Families are still coming. They're still buying tickets and paying for experiences. But they're doing it differently, more carefully, and the parks are caught between soaring demand and a wall of costs that won't budge.
what_changed:
The amusement park industry is experiencing real tension between robust demand and mounting cost pressure. Disney's domestic parks drew 76.5 million visitors in 2024 (up 0.6% year-over-year), and the opening of Universal's Epic Universe in May 2025—with five new themed worlds including Harry Potter's Ministry of Magic and Super Nintendo World—is projected to bring 5.2 million visitors in its opening year alone, climbing to 9.2 million by 2026. Comcast's Theme Parks segment generated $9.836 billion in full-year 2025 revenue, up 14.2% from 2024. This growth is what makes the headline look good. But the margins tell a different story. Labor costs now consume 35% of operating expenses, and wage inflation has stayed sticky at roughly 2.9% annually. Imported ride systems and equipment face tariff pressure. The combined Cedar Fair-Six Flags entity—formed in July 2024 to control 27 regional parks—carries a $5.5 billion debt load while attendance at those parks fell 1.4 million in Q2 2025 compared to the prior year. This is the bind: nominal revenue is climbing because parks have pricing power on headline tickets, but real per-guest margins are eroding.

Due to this pressure, parks are making contradictory moves that expose price elasticity concerns. Disney raised its peak-day ticket prices to $224 at Disneyland and over $200 at Magic Kingdom in October 2025—the first hike to the lowest-tier ticket ($104) in six years. But the company simultaneously offered its deepest discounts in years to maintain traffic, a strategy that signals guests are becoming visibly price-sensitive about the cost of a family vacation. The parks have made big capital commitments. Epic Universe represents a multi-billion-dollar bet, and regional parks have invested in new attractions and infrastructure. What's changed is that these investments must now contend with sticky labor costs, climate risk (Disney reported a $120 million operational impact from Hurricanes Helene and Milton in October 2024), and a consumer base that is still coming but shopping more carefully. The industry grew to 750 establishments by 2026 (a 7.0% CAGR from 2021), with employment of 244,202 as of 2022, but this growth is happening in a market where price elasticity has moved from invisible to obvious.

What became scarce is margin room and predictable attendance growth. What became newly valuable is operational efficiency, dynamic pricing (discounting deeper when needed), and franchising the theme-park experience beyond the gates—which explains both Universal's bet on Epic Universe's scale and smaller operators' struggle. The regional park sector, hit hardest by the Cedar Fair-Six Flags integration and debt burden, is being pruned of weaker assets and forced to compete on value and local draw rather than national destination appeal. Estimated margins sit at 10-12% industry-wide, but that figure masks wide variation: dominant players like Disney and Comcast can absorb tariff and labor costs through pricing power; regional operators cannot. What became risky is over-leveraged expansion and dependency on single-market visitors during climate seasons.

win: Disney and Comcast win because they own scale, brand loyalty, and the content that justifies high ticket prices. The Epic Universe expansion anchors Comcast's strategy to broaden revenue per visitor and extend the vacation duration. Premium and destination parks can still raise prices because families will pay to see brands and worlds they cannot find elsewhere—Harry Potter's Ministry of Magic, Super Nintendo World. They can also weather tariff and labor cost pressures that would sink smaller operators. Comcast's 14.2% revenue growth in 2025 reflects this advantage. Regional and destination parks owned by the Cedar Fair-Six Flags combined entity can survive as portfolio players but only by consolidating, shedding unprofitable assets, and focusing on local and seasonal draw where pricing power is lower but operational simplicity is higher.
lose: Regional amusement parks and single-market operators are squeezed. The Cedar Fair-Six Flags merger created scale but also a $5.5 billion debt load that leaves little room for margin compression. Q2 2025 attendance fell 1.4 million year-over-year for the combined entity, a sign that cost-cutting and debt service are forcing tough choices on maintenance, staffing, and new attractions. Families visiting regional parks are price-sensitive; they can't be upsold the way Disney guests can. Labor costs (35% of operating expenses) and tariff-driven equipment expenses are eroding margins that are already thin at 10-12% industry-wide. Smaller independent operators without portfolio diversification or scale purchasing power are most at risk; some will be forced to sell, merge, or close. Infrastructure vulnerability to climate events (Disney's $120 million 2024 hurricane impact) also falls hardest on operators without the balance sheet to absorb it.
worry: The biggest risk is that the price-elasticity wall is visible and approaching. Disney's simultaneous price hike and deepest discounting in October 2025 shows the company is already managing demand with both carrot and stick. If family vacation budgets tighten further—whether from recession, credit stress, or just fatigue—attendance will fall despite marketing. The regional park sector is especially vulnerable because it lacks brand moat and pricing power; if Epic Universe and Disney parks pull attendance and spending upward, regional parks will face margin compression without the scale to fight back. Climate infrastructure risk is also real and asymmetric: Disney can absorb a $120 million hurricane impact; most operators cannot. A concentrated destination-park model (Florida, Southern California, Orlando) also creates dependency on regional economic conditions and climate seasons, making the entire sector vulnerable to geographic shock.
one_sentence: Theme parks are growing revenue fast but the money is being squeezed by labor and equipment costs, leaving only the biggest players with room to raise prices—everyone else is stuck discounting to keep the gates full.

title: Staying & Celebrating
dek: The premium night costs more—labor, insurance, and real estate squeeze the industry while the chains swallow the boutiques.
one_sentence: Boutique hotels and casinos are becoming pricier as labor costs and operating expenses surge, squeezing independent owners while large operators consolidate and premium segments hold their ground.
lede: People want the special night—the boutique hotel stay, the casino weekend, the once-a-year celebration. But the price of delivering that experience keeps climbing. Labor is scarce and expensive. Insurance, utilities, and refinancing costs are eating away at what used to be comfortable margins. The old independent hoteliers who built this market are disappearing, and the big chains are moving in.
what_changed:
The boutique hotel market grew from 5,610 establishments in 2021 to a projected 8,724 by 2026—a 55% increase in properties over five years. But this explosive growth has a dark side: the independent owners who started it are getting pushed out, and the industry's profit margins are collapsing. Margins fell from 18.4% in 2016 to just 15.1% by 2021, and they've kept sliding as labor costs per occupied room jumped 21% between Q4 2024 and Q4 2025 alone (hitting $54.98 per room). The boutique hotel segment itself is now a huge piece of the luxury market—it held 53.5% of all luxury hotel revenue in 2025—but it's no longer a goldmine for the mom-and-pop owners. Major bankruptcies in late 2025 and early 2026 tell the story: Sonder, the boutique hotel tech startup that promised to disrupt the space, filed bankruptcy in November 2025 after Marriott cut ties; Revo Hospitality Group, operating 260 hotels, went into Chapter 11 in early 2026 as refinancing walls hit. Labor costs are now the killer—up 21% in a single year—and operating costs (insurance up 100%, utilities up 30%) are spiking even faster than revenue can climb. The chains realized the opportunity and moved in, launching collection brands like Hilton's Outset (60+ hotels in development) designed to soak up independent operators who want distribution without dying on the vine.

The US casino hotel industry tells a parallel story of consolidation and expense. At $84.6 billion in 2026, it's a mature market growing only 4.8% per year—essentially flat from 2025 to 2026. But the real action is vertical: labor is expensive (hotel staff wages rose 4-8% in 2025, and cost per occupied room jumped 12.8%), squeezing operator margins even when occupancy is strong. The number of casinos is creeping upward (575 expected by 2027, up from 492 in 2022), but the profit pool is thin and getting thinner. The mega-deals being struck tell the story of consolidation: Fertitta Entertainment offered $7 billion for Caesars Entertainment in a deal totaling $31.5 billion with debt, expected to close late 2026 or early 2027. VICI Properties, the real estate arm, is snapping up casino properties (Golden Portfolio, 7 casinos for $1.15 billion in April 2026; Gamehost Canada for $141 million in June 2026). MGM Resorts dumped $300 million into refreshing the MGM Grand Las Vegas (4,000 rooms renovated, finished November 2025) and reported 20% EBITDA growth in Q4 2025, but this premium-focused strategy only works if you're big enough to afford the capex.

The market is bifurcating by customer and by region. Premium Las Vegas resorts stay resilient—gaming revenue flat, but higher-value customers per room, so they can raise prices. Mid-tier regional casinos face slower foot traffic and must compete on price, which crushes margins for smaller operators. The one wild card is regulation: online casino legalization is spreading (Illinois, Indiana, and Maine moved bills forward in late 2025 and early 2026), and 38 states now have legal sports betting as of August 2026. But online gaming is not cannibalizing land-based casinos—instead, the biggest operators use digital platforms to funnel players into physical resorts via loyalty credits and promotional offers. This means online becomes a cost to acquire customers for expensive physical properties, which makes the cost of playing on land even higher.

win: The big chains and mega-operators win decisively. Marriott, Hilton, and MGM Resorts can absorb higher labor and operating costs because they're large enough to pass them on to premium customers and maintain volume across hundreds of properties. Fertitta Entertainment's $31.5 billion Caesars deal and VICI Properties' aggressive real estate plays show consolidation accelerating—only the biggest players have the capital to renovate 4,000 rooms at once (MGM Grand, November 2025) or bid $7 billion for a competitor. Premium Las Vegas resorts and high-end destination casinos thrive because their customers will pay for the experience; they can afford the cost inflation. The luxury boutique segment holding 53.5% of market revenue in 2025 shows customers still chase the premium night—they're just willing to pay chains for it rather than independents.
lose: The independent boutique hotel owner is getting crushed. The market grew from 5,610 properties in 2021 to 8,724 in 2026, but these new properties are mostly chain acquisitions or collection-brand properties, not mom-and-pop shops. Sonder's bankruptcy and Revo's Chapter 11 filing in late 2025 and early 2026 show how brutal the economics have become—even well-funded independents can't outrun labor costs rising 21% per room per year. Mid-tier and regional casino operators are squeezed by the same cost inflation (12.8% per room in 2025) but don't have the pricing power of premium Las Vegas to pass it through; they lose traffic to both online gaming and premium destination casinos, and must compete on price instead. Insurance up 100%, utilities up 30%—these hits hurt small operators far worse than large chains that can negotiate volume discounts.
worry: The biggest risk is that labor costs and operating expense inflation have decoupled from revenue growth. Boutique hotels are growing 6.99% annually but labor costs jumped 21% in a single year (Q4 2024 to Q4 2025). Casino hotels grew flat (4.8% projected CAGR through 2034) while costs rose 12.8% in one year. This math doesn't work indefinitely. Either prices rise sharply—which could choke demand from the middle-class customers who chase the boutique experience and weekend casino trip—or margins continue to compress and more independents fail. The second risk is that regulatory expansion of online casinos and sports betting (38 states now legal, growing through 2026) will force operators to invest heavily in digital acquisition and loyalty programs just to maintain physical traffic, shifting the casino experience from a place you go to have fun into an expensive customer-acquisition funnel that's most cost-effective only for the biggest operators.

title: The big screen fights back
dek: Theaters and live events survive by being an experience streaming can't copy—and they're pricing for it.
lede: Streaming killed casual moviegoing and made concerts too expensive for most people. But theater and event companies learned to survive anyway—not by serving everyone, but by serving the moments that matter most. They've turned the experience into a premium product, and consumers who care enough are paying for it.
what_changed:
Movie theaters hit bottom in 2024 but never fully climbed back. The US theater market sat at $8.6 to $8.8 billion in 2025—still down 23 to 27 percent below the 2019 pre-pandemic peak. Total ticket volume collapsed: 1.225 billion admissions in 2019 fell to 780 million in 2025, a 34 percent drop that won't reverse. What survived, though, tells the real story. Attendance split into two modes: blockbuster events like Inside Out 2 and Deadpool & Wolverine pack theaters. Everything else fails. Generic midbudget films die at the box office. This bifurcation forced a structural change. Studios learned that a 26-to-45-day theatrical window maximizes both box office revenue and downstream streaming dollars—something that didn't exist five years ago. CinemaCon 2026 saw every major studio commit to at least 45-day theatrical exclusivity. Universal extended to 7 weekends by 2027. Theater became something streaming needed, not something streaming killed.

The chains that survived rebuilt themselves around margins, not volume. AMC emerged from years of near-collapse with Q2-2026 EBITDA margins hitting 20 percent—triple the industry average of 7.3 percent. Cinemark reported 18.6 percent margins in 2025. Both did this by closing hundreds of unprofitable locations, consolidating their footprint, and raising ticket prices 5.7 percent in 2025. The weak players—iPic, LOOK, CMX—filed bankruptcy between 2024 and 2026. Theater count has dropped, but per-theater economics improved sharply. The remaining 2,200 enterprises are fighting a different war: not making movies accessible, but making certain screenings unmissable.

Concerts swung the opposite direction: booming, but hollowed out. The concert and event promotion industry hit $60.2 billion in 2026, up 7.4 percent from 2024, on record attendance and soaring ticket prices. Live Nation Entertainment alone posted record revenue of $25.2 billion in 2025, a 9 percent year-over-year jump, with 159 million fans attending 55,000 concerts globally. But money concentrated sharply. Concert ticket prices soared to an average of $144 in 2025, up 45 percent since 2019. Dynamic pricing algorithms (Ticketmaster's, primarily) pushed consumers toward extreme spending: 36 percent were willing to pay $100 to $499 per ticket, and 17 percent willing to spend up to $1,000. Yet venues below the superstar tier collapsed. Rockwood Music Hall, an iconic NYC independent venue, closed in November 2024. Avant Gardner in Brooklyn filed for bankruptcy owing $155 million in debt. The Music Hall of Williamsburg faced eviction at the end of 2026. UK grassroots venues closed at one every two weeks. The revenue growth masked a winner-take-most market where Live Nation and Ticketmaster controlled 86 percent of primary ticketing at major venues, used that control to bundle promotions with amphitheater access, and systematized overcharges of $1.72 per ticket. In April 2026, a federal jury found them liable on all antitrust counts. Damages could exceed $450 million if trebled. Yet the industry kept growing—because the top 1 percent of events still pulled in massive spending, and the middle tier simply died.

evidence: Movie theaters: US chain AMC reported Q2-2026 EBITDA margin of 20% on $1.6B revenue (+14.2% YoY), after shuttering 200+ unprofitable locations during 2024-2025 consolidation.
Concerts: Average US concert ticket prices hit $144 in 2025 (up 45% from 2019), with Live Nation reporting record $25.2B revenue on 159M fans at 55,000 concerts globally in 2025.
Streaming shift: Studios committed to 45-day minimum theatrical windows at CinemaCon 2026 after research showed 26-45 day windows maximize both box office and downstream SVOD revenue.
Consolidation: US theater chains fell to ~2,200 enterprises with 193,000 employees; iPic, LOOK, CMX filed Chapter 11 (2024-2026); Cinemark survived with 18.6% EBITDA margin (2025).

Venue collapse: Independent concert venues—Rockwood Music Hall (NYC), Avant Gardner (Brooklyn), The Music Hall of Williamsburg (Brooklyn)—filed bankruptcy or faced eviction in 2024-2026, while Ticketmaster maintained 86% market share at major venues (April 2026 antitrust verdict).
win: Theater chains that cut locations and raised margins win—AMC and Cinemark now operate slimmer, higher-margin businesses focused on blockbuster events and premium formats. Concert promoters riding the top tier of a winner-take-most market win big: Live Nation hit record revenue while the entire grassroots venue sector collapsed. Studios win by getting theatrical windows back as a window into streaming—the window is now a feature, not a threat.
lose: Casual moviegoers and mid-tier concert fans lose. Theater attendance dropped 34 percent overall, and those with modest budgets face ticket prices that have climbed to $144 for concerts and premium formats for films. Independent venues—the 1,000s of small music halls, art houses, and specialty theaters—are dying faster than they're being born. Smaller concert promoters and independent artists lose direct access to fans as Live Nation's bundle of promotions and venue access squeezes them out. The 64 percent of concert-goers who can't justify $100+ tickets priced themselves out of the market.
worry: The biggest risk is that the premium experience economy bifurcates completely—blockbuster events and superstar concerts thrive while everything else withers. If ticket prices keep rising 45 percent per decade and consolidation keeps squeezing independent venues, live experiences stop being a mass market and become a luxury good for the top 20 percent of income earners. Meanwhile, streaming gets stronger, SVOD subscriber bases locked in at 2.2 billion globally (2x pre-pandemic), and the regulatory heat on Live Nation and Ticketmaster could fracture the business before the true middle market has a chance to rebuild.
one_sentence: The big screen and live events survive by abandoning the middle market—they now serve blockbusters and superstars at premium prices, while independent venues and casual fans disappear.

title: The Experience Economy
dek: Spending shifts decisively from ownership to spectacle—who's riding the wave and who's drowning in it.
lede: The American consumer is remaking the budget. From 2022 to 2026, the money moving to amusement parks, bars, boutique hotels, and premium entertainment is reshaping which businesses thrive and which disappear. Ownership of things was the 20th-century middle-class dream. Experiences—memories, status, escape—are becoming the new measure of living well. And that shift is brutal for some industries and lucrative for others.
what_changed:
The experience economy made one thing newly precious: the moment itself. When people chose to spend $33.4 billion at amusement parks in 2026 (up 9.7% CAGR since 2022), they were voting for spectacle over spare bedrooms. Disney's parks pulled in 76.5 million domestic visitors in 2024, and Universal's Epic Universe alone is projected to hit 9.2 million visits by 2026. The sheer attendance numbers tell the real story: people are willing to pay premiums—peak Disney tickets hit $224 at Disneyland in October 2025—for the promise of escape, memory, status. Amusement parks grew from $14.3 billion in 2022 to $33.4 billion in 2026, and the number of establishments jumped 7.0% annually. What this force made valuable was scale, innovation, and the ability to charge repeatedly for the same customer across a season or year.

What it made scarce was commodity appeal. Bars and nightclubs still command $38.6 billion in revenue in 2026, but real margins have compressed from 6.8% in 2022 to 5.4% by 2026. Younger drinkers are drinking less (65% of Gen Z report intent to reduce alcohol in 2025) but paying more when they do—selective premiumization. Labor costs in a typical nightclub run $70,416 per month with 50-70% annual bartender turnover, so venue owners face an impossible choice: cut service quality to preserve margin, or absorb wage inflation and hope themed experiences (up 32.9% in 2025) and alcohol-free cocktails (up 36% year-over-year) attract enough new traffic. Meanwhile, imported spirits tariffs lifted prices 15-20% above 2024 levels by mid-2026, hitting premium bottle service hardest. The bifurcation is real: upscale cocktail lounges with experiential design and strong customer loyalty are winning; casual drinks-to-go and moderation-focused venues are losing.

Boutique hotels show the same pattern in sharper relief. The luxury boutique segment held 53.5% of market revenue in 2025 with occupancy holding at 70-75% and RevPAR up 5.3%. But the independents who invented the category are vanishing. Sonder, the tech-enabled boutique hotel pioneer, filed for bankruptcy in November 2025 after Marriott terminated its deal. Revo Hospitality Group (260 hotels) filed Chapter 11 in early 2026. Fairmont collapsed under its own maturity wall. What changed is ownership. Marriott, Hilton, and other global chains now own the independent-hotel fantasy. Hilton launched its Outset Collection with 60+ properties in development targeting independent owners. Airbnb, once a disruptive threat, now partners directly with boutique hotels in New York, Los Angeles, Madrid, and San Francisco. This force made authentic, curated hospitality valuable—and made it profitable only at scale or under brand control. Labor costs per occupied room jumped 21% from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025 (to $54.98), while operating costs surged: insurance up 100%, utilities up 30%. Margins compressed from 18.4% in 2016 to 15.1% by 2026.

Movie theaters reveal the harshest truth about experience spending: it is radically bifurcated. Attendance fell 34% from 2019 to 2025 (1.225 billion tickets down to 780 million), but event films—Inside Out 2, Deadpool & Wolverine—still filled seats. The industry bounced to $8.6-8.8 billion in 2025, but only because studios and chains made hard structural moves. AMC shuttered 200+ theaters. iPic, LOOK, and CMX filed bankruptcy. Cinemark and Regal, the survivors, negotiated longer theatrical windows (45 days or more by 2026) with studios to capture both box office and downstream streaming value. Ticket prices rose 5.7% in 2025 to offset attendance loss. What this force made valuable is authenticity and occasion—seeing a film with friends, in a theater, for a movie event worth the trip. What it made cheap is everyday, casual moviegoing. A Wednesday matinee in suburbia is now a loss leader. Premium formats (IMAX, Dolby, 3D), blockbuster events, and consolidated theater chains are what survived the 2019-2026 reckoning.

evidence: Amusement Parks: $33.4B market in 2026 with 9.7% CAGR, 750 establishments, and Disney reporting 76.5M domestic visitors in 2024 despite peak tickets reaching $224

Bars & Nightclubs: $38.6B revenue in 2026 (1.5% annualized growth through 2030) with margins falling to 5.4% from 6.8% in 2022, while labor costs per typical venue run $70,416/month and spirits tariffs added 15-20% by mid-2026

Boutique Hotels: $76.3B market in 2026 with luxury segment holding 53.5% of revenue, but independent owners collapsing (Sonder bankruptcy Nov 2025, Revo Chapter 11 early 2026) as labor costs jumped 21% YoY and operating costs exploded (insurance +100%, utilities +30%)

Movie Theaters: $8.6-8.8B in 2025 on 780M admissions, down 34% from 2019, with consolidation (AMC closed 200+ theaters, iPic/LOOK/CMX bankrupt) and studios locking in 45-day theatrical windows to compete with 1.1B SVOD subscribers

Experience Bifurcation: Gen Z drinking down 65% intent reduction yet consumption up to 73%; themed bars +32.9% in 2025; alcohol-free cocktails +36% YoY; selective premiumization across all venue types
win: Theme park operators, luxury hotel chains, and consolidated theater companies win decisively. Disney and Universal control the destination experience narrative and command pricing power (Disney's $224 tickets despite price sensitivity). Marriott and Hilton absorb independent boutique hotels through branded collections (Hilton's Outset Collection, 60+ in pipeline). AMC and Cinemark, the surviving theater chains, use consolidation to negotiate directly with studios, lock in longer theatrical windows, and charge premiums for immersive formats. For bars, only upscale venues with strong brand identity and experiential design (themed bars, craft cocktails, alcohol-free innovation) are thriving. The common thread: scale, brand control, and the ability to create occasion and memory at premium pricing. Chains beat independents every time.
lose: Independent hotel owners and small boutique operators face extinction. Sonder's bankruptcy in November 2025 and Revo's Chapter 11 in early 2026 signal the end of the independent era. Casual movie theaters and suburban multiplex chains are closed or closing (AMC alone shuttered 200+, and iPic, LOOK, and CMX filed bankruptcy). Economy hotel segments are declining as luxury boutique dominates. Local and independent bars face margin collapse (down to 5.4% from 6.8%) as chains consolidate and tariffs and labor costs rise. Regional amusement parks (Cedar Fair-Six Flags merger brought $5.5B debt and down 1.4M visitors in Q2 2025) struggle under high operating costs and competition from destination parks. Small movie theater operators with no scale to negotiate studio windows or invest in premium formats are simply gone. The losers share one trait: lack of scale or brand power to negotiate costs, set prices, or create occasion at premium points.
worry: The experience economy rests on willingness to pay, and that willingness has limits. Disney's simultaneous price increases to $224 and deeper discounts in October 2025 reveal the danger: consumers are price-sensitive about family vacations even as they spend on experiences. Gen Z's stated intent to reduce drinking (65%) contradicts actual consumption, suggesting delayed adjustment or an uncomfortable divergence between aspiration and behavior. The Cedar Fair-Six Flags merger produced a $5.5 billion debt load with declining attendance (down 1.4M in Q2 2025). Recession, inflation of experiences themselves (ticket prices up, cocktails up, hotel rooms up), or a drop in discretionary income could collapse the experience economy faster than it rose. The real risk: experience spending survives only if it remains a luxury for the affluent and selective premiumization for the middle class. If access becomes genuinely expensive (theater tickets, hotel rooms, park admissions), the volume game breaks and margins evaporate. Scale plays work today because volume is still there. Scale breaks when volume stops.
one_sentence: Scale and brand control are eating the experience economy, leaving room only for big operators who can charge premium prices while independents vanish into bankruptcy.
